title: Nine random holes beat a grid
allegory: A sweep is like digging for treasure buried in a long north-south stripe: nine holes on a 3×3 grid test only three east-west spots, while nine random holes test nine.
map: east-west position, which decides whether you hit treasure
the one hyperparameter that really matters, e.g. learning rate
a hyperparameter the metric hardly depends on
one training run in the sweep
a flag on each hole noting where and what was found
wandb.log: every run's config and metrics in one table
credit: The 'try random values, don't use a grid' picture and sampling the learning rate on a log scale (lr = 10^r) follow Andrew Ng's framing in the Deep Learning Specialization, Course 2, hyperparameter tuning.

props.label: which lr was the good one?

cap.1: Train more than one model and the hard part becomes bookkeeping. Which run had which settings? Which one was actually good?
cap.2: W&B is four calls in your loop: wandb.init, watch, log, finish. Every run lands in one table with its config attached, ready to sort and compare.
cap.3: init(project, name, config); watch(model, log_freq) for gradient and parameter histograms; log(metrics, step); finish() always, even after a crash. A library call: learn the four, move on.

cap.1: You may dig nine holes. The treasure lies in a long north-south stripe, so only how far east you dig matters. Where should the holes go?
cap.2: Two hyperparameters, nine runs, and only one of them really moves the metric. That is the usual situation, and it decides how to spend the budget.
cap.3: Bergstra and Bengio (JMLR 2012): hyperparameter importance is highly uneven, so the search has low effective dimensionality. The layout of trials should respect that.

chapters.name: Grid versus random

right.title: 9 random holes
lines: far likelier to hit the stripe

chapters.verdict: Same budget, three times the coverage on the axis that matters.

cap.1: A 3×3 grid digs each east-west spot three times, varying only the direction that does not matter. Nine random holes try nine different spots.
cap.2: A grid of k values per axis explores only k distinct values of the important hyperparameter, however many runs it spends. Random sampling gets a fresh value every run.
cap.3: Projected onto the important axis, a grid collapses to k points while random trials stay n distinct points. Hence method: 'random' in the ARENA sweep config. A grid is still fine for one or two knobs.

cap.1: Squash the field onto the east-west line. The grid only ever tried three spots, and here the sweet spot sits between them.
cap.2: Score against the one hyperparameter that matters. The grid's three values straddle the peak; nine random values would scatter across it.
cap.3: Marginalise onto the important axis: the grid's projection is 3 points whatever the budget; a random design's is n points, so the odds of landing near a narrow optimum grow with n.

cap.1: For learning rates the power of ten is what matters. So pick the power at random, not the number: each decade from 0.00001 to 0.1 gets a fair share.
cap.2: In the sweep config: distribution: 'log_uniform_values' with min 1e-5, max 1e-1. Plain uniform sampling would put about 90% of runs above 1e-2.
cap.3: log(lr) ~ Uniform(log min, log max) is the natural prior for a scale parameter. Linear-uniform over [1e-5, 1e-1] puts 90% of its mass in the top decade alone.

chapters.name: The sweep that wasn't
chapters.note: the table says it varied. the model says it didn't.

cap.1: The table lists nine different settings, yet all nine runs draw the same curve. The sweep chose settings; your code never read them.
cap.2: The agent writes sampled values to wandb.config, but train() still builds args from a hard-coded dataclass. Call wandb.init(), then build args from wandb.config.
cap.3: The logged config is the sampled one; the trained config is the default. Build args from wandb.config after init, assert one sampled value on the first batch, and call finish() in a finally block.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: SAE runs: read L0, explained variance and dead latents together
Log-uniform for rates, random for the rest
A sweep needs your judgement to aim it

cap.1: Later you will train sparse autoencoders to look inside models, and you will judge each run by three logged curves side by side.
cap.2: In [1.3.3] SAE runs log L0, explained variance and dead-latent count to W&B. Reading the three together is how you tell a good dictionary from a bad one.
cap.3: SAE quality is a trade-off between sparsity, reconstruction and dead latents, compared across logged runs. That is how you choose the lens you then use to understand and steer models.

caption.1: Drag the sweet spot along the field and make it narrower. Which bars light up: the grid's three spots or the nine random ones? Usually random wins, not always.
caption.2: Each bar is one distinct learning rate a search tried. The grid spends nine runs on three values; random spends nine on nine. Park the peak on a grid value to watch the grid win.
caption.3: Best-of-n along the important axis: the grid gets 3 distinct draws, random gets 9. For narrow optima random's expected best is far higher, though any single layout can lose.

hamming.what: Weights & Biases logs every run's config and metrics in one place, and a sweep samples configs and launches the runs for you.
hamming.when: As soon as you train more than one model, and whenever you tune learning rate, weight decay or batch size.
hamming.why: Only a few hyperparameters usually matter, so random sampling covers them better than a grid, and logging makes the winner findable and reproducible.

object.title: The treasure field
object.subtitle: A score landscape with a ridge only one knob controls, pinned with grid holes and random holes.

cap.1: A field of settings; height is how well the run scores. The ridge runs front to back, so only the left-right knob matters.
cap.2: Score over two hyperparameters. It depends almost entirely on one of them.
cap.3: An objective with low effective dimensionality: nearly constant along y, peaked along x.

cap.1: From above: nine grid pins in three tidy columns, nine random pins scattered everywhere.
cap.2: The two designs, same budget: a 3×3 lattice and nine independent samples.
cap.3: Lattice versus i.i.d. uniform design, n = 9 each.

cap.1: Look straight along the ridge. The grid's nine pins pile onto just three spots; the random nine stay nine different spots.
cap.2: Seen end-on, the grid tried three learning rates and random tried nine.
cap.3: Projection onto the important axis: 3 distinct grid values versus 9 random ones.

cap.1: Make the sweet spot narrow. Every grid pin now misses it, while one random pin still lands close.
cap.2: A narrow optimum between grid lines is simply invisible to the grid.
cap.3: As the optimum narrows, the grid's best-of-3 collapses faster than random's best-of-9.

cap.1: Honest caveat: slide the ridge onto a grid column and the grid wins. Random is better on average, not every time.
cap.2: When the optimum happens to sit on a grid value, the grid hits it exactly.
cap.3: Random dominates in expectation over optimum location, not pointwise; any fixed design has lucky placements.

predict.q: Nine runs on a 3×3 grid over two hyperparameters. How many distinct learning rates get tried?
predict.why: A grid repeats each value along the other axis. Nine random samples would try nine distinct learning rates.

predict.q: Your sweep table shows nine different configs, but all nine loss curves are identical. Most likely cause?

options.t: train() builds args from a hard-coded dataclass, not wandb.config

predict.why: The agent writes sampled values to wandb.config; if train() never reads them, every run trains the same model.

predict.q: Why sample a learning rate log-uniformly between 1e-5 and 1e-1?

options.t: The order of magnitude is what matters, so each decade should get equal runs
Because smaller learning rates are always better

predict.why: Uniform sampling would put about 90% of runs above 1e-2; log-uniform gives each of the four decades a quarter.

object.where: Any search where few knobs matter: random probes cover the important axis better than a lattice.
